title: Emaki 絵巻
section: From the IDE to the ADE
text:
From the IDE to the ADE





IDE integrated development environment

IDEs are made for hand crafting, with numerous panels and a steep learning curve. In agentic workflows, the chat does most of the work, yet the editor still takes the middle of the screen and the chat gets a narrow pane at the edge.







ADE agentic development environment

Emaki turns this around, and we call it ADE. The agent chat takes the main space, and the sidebar groups your sessions under their projects. The rest stays hidden until you need it: the files and a terminal in panels at the chat’s sides, and in its margins the outline and your agent’s own CLI.

title: Emaki 絵巻
text:
Main system
Sessions are listed and managed under their projects. The agent chat takes the main space, rendered in high quality.

title: Emaki 絵巻
text:
Panels
Two panels stand at the chat’s sides, hidden until you need them, since they are essential but used less often than the chat: the files at the left and a terminal at the right, each from a button at an end of the strip over the chat.

title: Emaki 絵巻
text:
Margins
On each side of the agent chat, you can hover and toggle 2 more panels. The left margin gives you the outline panel with quick jumping and summarizing; the right margin lets you switch between the rendered UI and the original CLI.

title: Settings ⌘,
text: Your avatar and name, the window’s theme, and its accent: Periwinkle, Orchid, Rose, Amber, Moss, Jade or Teal. The list at the right of the section’s name picks the window’s language, from eight. Under Power, a switch keeps the display on while a session works.

title: Settings ⌘,
text: Your avatar and name, the window’s theme, and its accent: Periwinkle, Orchid, Rose, Amber, Moss, Jade or Teal. The list at the right of the section’s name picks the window’s language, from eight. Under Power, a switch keeps the display on while a session works.

title: Settings ⌘,
text:
Text
Two pages, Fonts and Size, chosen at the right of the section’s name.

Fonts



Eight faces for the chat, four serif and four sans serif, and four monospace faces for code and the terminals.


Size



Small, Medium and Large set every place at once. Custom is your own set: each place’s size, stepped a point at a time or typed.

title: Settings ⌘,
text:
Conversation



How the chat draws the agent’s work: three or more tool calls in a row fold into one row that opens, and the Outline can be turned off. Then the composer: the key that sends, auto-capitalization, and spelling and grammar checked as you type, in US or UK English, Spanish, French or German. Spanish, French and German are checked on a Mac only.

title: Settings ⌘,
text:
Model calls



Everything Emaki asks a small model for, each a call on your account: the plain-word explanations of tool calls, and the Outline’s labels and summaries. Each has a switch, and each agent has a model to choose for them, from its own list.

title: Settings ⌘,
text:
New sessions



Each agent’s permission mode, model and effort for a new session. The pills under the composer change them for one session (Chats).

title: Settings ⌘,
text:
Panels



Which side each goes on: the Files Panel and the Terminal Panel, one at each side of the chat, and in its margins the Outline’s seam and the layout’s, which brings in the Agent CLI. Each pair is one choice, in the order they stand from left to right.

title: Settings ⌘,
text:
Files



Whether a file opens as it reads or as it is written, and format on save with the languages it covers, each with its own formatter.

title: Settings ⌘,
text:
Terminal



The terminal’s theme, its cursor, ligatures and copy on select. Its face is set in Fonts and its size in Size.

title: Settings ⌘,
text:
Shortcuts



The keys of the window’s commands, in two lists: the window’s, Sessions and Panels, and the file editor’s Sublime Text commands, Lines and Text. Click a command’s keys and press new ones; a key already taken is refused, and a button puts a changed key back. The Keys page lists them as they begin.

title: Settings ⌘,
text:
About
Who makes Emaki, the version, and updates: Emaki checks once a day, and installs nothing without you.

title: Outline ⌘⇧O
text: Going back through a long session is a pain. The Outline lists every round of the chat under its day, each with its time and a short label of what came of it, written by a small model of your agent’s, the one Settings, Model calls names for it. Click an entry to scroll back to its round.

title: Outline ⌘⇧O
text:
The drawer
The Outline lives in the chat’s left margin. Move the pointer there and a seam appears, a line down the margin with a knob halfway. Click the knob, or press ⌘⇧O, and the drawer slides out, the chat moving over for it; click again to put it away. It belongs to the chat: switching to the Agent CLI folds it away, and the chat brings it back as it was.

title: Outline ⌘⇧O
text:
Summaries
Summarize session, under the entries, writes a summary of the session in bullets and heads the entries with sections. Update brings it up to date from the new rounds alone, and Hide puts it away. The Outline summaries switch in Settings, Model calls turns the labels and summaries off while keeping the Outline.
Each label and summary is a call to a small model of your agent’s, on your account. Settings turns them off, which keeps the Outline without them, and chooses the model for each agent. Settings, Conversation, turns the Outline itself off.

title: Get Started
text:
Open a project
Choose a folder, pick an agent, and type your first prompt. That starts a session in the folder, with a tab and a row in the sidebar. To pick up an older one, find it in the sidebar: every session on this computer is listed under its project, from both agents.
On the first launch, Emaki copies every Claude Code session into ~/.emaki/archive, and each later launch catches up, so a session Claude Code has deleted is still here. See Projects.

title: Get Started
text:
Layout
The sidebar and the chat are always there. Two panels are hidden until you need them: the Files Panel opens at the chat’s left and the Terminal Panel at its right, each from a button at an end of the strip over the chat. Two more things wait in the chat’s margins. The Outline is a drawer that slides out into the left margin, and the Agent CLI, your agent’s own screen, takes the chat’s place from the right margin and gives it back. Each has a seam in its margin, a line with a knob halfway, which shows when the pointer comes near. Settings puts each on the side you choose.





Projects


Chats


Files ⌘⇧F


Outline ⌘⇧O


Terminal ⌘⇧S


Agent CLI ⌘⇧L

title: Get Started
text:
What Emaki keeps
Everything Emaki keeps is in ~/.emaki:







archive/
every Claude Code session, copied byte for byte


logs/
each session rendered as markdown


search.db
the full-text index


config.json
your settings



Codex has its own archiving system, so archive/ only stores Claude Code sessions.
Emaki changes one setting in Claude Code: its status line, which feeds Emaki’s own status line under the composer. To put yours back, run emaki-core statusline restore.

title: Chats
text:
Transcript
Chat transcripts are well-rendered with high-quality interface. Agent tool calls are stacked to release reading pressure. You can expand them and even get summaries of each tool call to understand what happened. Artifacts, background jobs, subagents, Q&A sessions are all properly taken care of with smooth UI.

title: Chats
text:
Margins
The chat’s two margins each hold a seam, a line down the margin with a knob halfway, shown while the pointer is near. The left one slides out the Outline, a drawer of every round. The right one switches the chat for the Agent CLI, your agent’s own screen, and back. Settings puts each on the side you choose.

title: Chats
text:
Composer
Attach files by pasting, dropping, or the + button. @ picks a file or folder from the project, and / lists the agent’s slash commands and skills. A message that starts with ! runs as a shell command in the project’s folder, and the chat shows it with its output. Spelling and grammar are checked as you type.

We proudly recommend using Kotoba as your dictation app on Emaki or any other composer on your machine. It supports light-weighted models for voice-to-text dictation and post-processing.

title: Chats
text:
Mode, model and effort
By providing three pills under the composer, Emaki made it easy to toggle among different modes, models, and efforts without needing to trigger keyboard commands or / commands (though they are also supported).

title: Chats
text:
Status line
The row under the composer shows how much of the context window is used and where the 5-hour and 7-day limits stand. Its colors change according to the thresholds. The status line logic is from the Waza plugin by tw93.

title: About
text:
The name
An emaki (絵巻) is a Japanese picture handscroll: a long painted scene held between two rolls, read by winding it from one to the other. It is colorful, enchanting, and easy to handle.
Our aim with Emaki is to give you the same experience: a colorful, enchanting, and easy-to-use studio for your agent sessions, with clear guidance, supportive panels, and small, versatile features for a smooth development experience.

title: About
text:
Our motivation
Emaki started with the pain of managing numerous agent sessions.
Working with agents has become the way many of us develop software. But as sessions pile up, managing them becomes a pain, especially with several agents, each storing its sessions its own way on your computer. Emaki helps you manage them: you can create, continue, archive, and delete sessions in one place.
Claude Code silently deletes its sessions after 30 days. Emaki archives them automatically, and you can continue one by unarchiving it.
From there, we made Emaki much more versatile. It has grown into an ADE, an agentic development environment, because we believe it is a better way to work with agents than the traditional IDE.

title: About
text:
App structure
Emaki is written in Rust, with GPUI, the Zed editor’s UI framework, and gpui-component for the window.
crates/emaki-core   core logic
crates/emaki-app    the window
vendor/             gpui, modified to meet our needs
docs/               how each part is built
scripts/            miscellaneous

title: About
text:
Meet the team



Alkaline Software
Alkaline Software is a development team of two engineers and data scientists, John Paul Helveston and Pingfan Hu, who enjoy building “basic” software. Alkaline means “basic” (a high pH), and basic is what our software is meant to be: things that should plainly exist. Emaki is one of them, a development environment for the agentic era that anyone who works with agents can use.

title: About
text:
Credits

Figures are based on the line-drawing manner of hairline’s figures, with our own modifications.
In-app icons are taken from Tabler’s outline set, with our own modifications.
The file tree’s icons are from Catppuccin.
The code colors are Rosé Pine’s hues, retinted for contrast.
The terminal keeps Kaku’s cream in the light appearance.
Every face the app carries is under the SIL Open Font License, and so are this site’s: Source Serif 4, JetBrains Mono and Belleza.
The site is made with Quarto.

title: Agent CLI ⌘⇧L
text:
If you want your agent’s original CLI, this is it. The Agent CLI is Claude Code’s or Codex’s own screen, running the same session, and it takes the chat’s place. Move the pointer to the chat’s right margin and a seam appears, a line down the margin with a knob halfway. Click the knob, or press ⌘⇧L, and the terminal slides in over the chat; the same seam switches back. The app calls the two the CLI layout and the rendered layout, and each tab keeps the one you chose for it.
A message typed in either shows in the other, so you can continue the session in whichever you like. As in the Terminal Panel, you can use your mouse, scrolling, and keyboard shortcuts. The Outline folds away with the chat and comes back with it.



 Back to top

title: Files Panel ⌘⇧F
text:
File tree
The Files Panel opens from the button at the left end of the strip over the chat, and stays open or closed across launches. The file tree is shown with its root folder expanded. Folders and files are drawn with Catppuccin’s file icons. If the project is a git repository, its changes are shown on the folders and files. The file tree supports mouse dragging and common keyboard shortcuts.

title: Files Panel ⌘⇧F
text:
File preview & editing
Click a file to open it in a pane between the tree and the chat; click it again to close it. Markdown, Quarto, LaTeX and Typst documents open rendered, and ⌘⇧V switches a file between its rendered and raw views. The enlarge button gives the pane the chat’s room. You can use common keyboard shortcuts to undo, redo, save, and close.
Emaki supports format on save for common languages. It is off by default and can be turned on in Settings: tick all the languages, or only the ones you want.
Supported file types:


Code
Markdown
LaTeX
Typst
CSV and TSV
Parquet
Word
Excel
PowerPoint
PDF
HTML
Pictures

title: Files Panel ⌘⇧F
text:
Git
If the project is a git repository, the git buttons appear in the Files Panel’s header. Click the branch name to switch branches or create a new one (⌘⇧N). You can also fetch, pull, and push from there.
The Changes pill (⌘⇧G) opens the Changes sheet. There you can review your changes, write a commit message, commit (⌘↩︎), and push (⌘P). The sheet’s History side lists your past commits.

title: Keys
text: ⌘ on macOS, Ctrl elsewhere.

title: Keys
text:
Panels
Hold ⇧ with ⌘, and the letter shows or hides something beside the chat, or switches what shows. The letter is the thing’s first, and B is the sidebar’s.







⌘⇧B
the sidebar, with your projects and their sessions; ⌘B too


⌘⇧F
Files Panel


⌘⇧S
Terminal Panel


⌘⇧O
the Outline’s drawer


⌘⇧L
the layout: the Agent CLI in the chat’s place, or the chat


⌘⇧G
git’s Changes sheet


⌘⇧V
a file in the Files Panel as it reads, or as it is written

title: Keys
text:
Pages
⌘ and a letter opens a page or a sheet over the window.







⌘K
search every session


⌘N
new session


⌘T
new session in this project


⌘O
choose a folder


⌘L
All Sessions


⌘E
Agents


⌘,
Settings



The rest of ⌘ each does one thing where you are.







⌘F · ⌘G
find in this chat, and the next hit; ⌘⇧G is the previous while the find bar is open


⌘↩︎
send, or commit in the Changes sheet


⌘P
push, in the Changes sheet


⌘S
save the file


⌘1 to ⌘9
tabs


⌘W · ⌘⇧T
close a tab, reopen the last


⌘⇧N
new branch


⌘R
refresh


Esc
stop, or close what is open



In the terminal, ⌘T or ⌘N opens a tab, ⌘W closes it and ⌘K clears the screen.

title: Keys
text:
Your own
Settings, Shortcuts, changes the keys of the window’s commands above, and of the file editor’s Sublime Text commands. A key already taken is refused, and a button puts a changed key back.

title: Projects
text:
Projects
All sessions in Emaki are project-based, all listed in the sidebar. You can pin your selected projects and show or hide sessions. To start a new session, you can either click the + button on an existing project or press ⌘T in the project you are in. With ⌘N, you can start one anywhere (the same as going to your landing page).
Put away (⌘⇧B), the sidebar folds to a rail of icons: search, New Session, All Sessions, Agents, and Projects, which opens your projects beside the rail until you choose one.

title: Projects
text:
Sessions

In the sidebar
Sessions are managed under their projects. A session’s leading logo tells you which agent it belongs to and lights up while the agent runs. A dot shows where the session stands: orange while a question waits for you, blue while the agent works or something it started still runs, green for half an hour after it finishes. A bar at the left marks a session that is open in a tab. Claude Code and Codex sessions sit side by side, each read from the agent’s own files.


All Sessions
All Sessions (⌘L) lists every project and session with the day it was last used. This page provides plenty of ways of easily managing your existing sessions.

title: Projects
text:
Archiving
Claude Code deletes its transcripts after 30 days. Emaki copies each one into ~/.emaki/archive. Codex never deletes sessions by age, so Emaki reads them in place.
An archived session is kept but not continued until you unarchive it. You can archive and unarchive sessions yourself. An unarchived Claude Code session goes back to Claude Code dated now, so its thirty days start again.

title: Projects
text:
Tabs
Each open session is a tab, grouped by project. ⌘1 to ⌘9 switch tabs, ⌘W closes one, ⌘⇧T reopens the last one closed, and you can drag tabs to reorder them.

title: Terminal Panel ⌘⇧S
text:
Opening a terminal and cd-ing to the project is easy, but doing it again and again is a pain. Emaki solves it for you! The Terminal Panel gives you terminal tabs that open in the project’s folder, from the button at the right end of the strip over the chat. Use the + button or ⌘T to open a new tab, and ⌘W to close one. Inside the terminal, you can use your mouse, scrolling, and keyboard shortcuts. On Windows and Linux the keys are your system terminal’s: Ctrl with a letter goes to the shell, and the panel’s own keys add Shift (Ctrl⇧T, Ctrl⇧W, Ctrl⇧C, Ctrl⇧V).
Its look is inspired by Kaku, in the window’s own colors and font.
